title: “It’s just the iron”
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative. The heparin order, any change to it, and blood-thinner decisions belong to the attending nephrologist and the prescribers; your unit’s protocol sets every number.
intro: You are the physician on duty. Mr. Rogelio Santos, 66, dialyzes through a fistula. He takes clopidogrel after a coronary stent eight months ago, and oral iron. At 06:40 the nurse is about to give the heparin bolus. While she asks the gate questions, he mentions his stool has been black and sticky for two days. “It’s just the iron, Doc.”

choices.text: Count it as a “yes”: hold the bolus, check him, call the nephrologist.
choices.feedback: Iron darkens stool, but black, sticky stool can also be blood from the upper gut, and he is on an antiplatelet drug. Any “yes” at the gate holds the bolus until the attending nephrologist has heard. Look and measure while you call.
choices.then: Sitting, his pulse is 88; standing, 108, and he feels light-headed. A point-of-care hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL.

choices.text: Give the bolus as ordered. Iron is the likely cause, and you can ask about his stool again at the end of the session.
choices.feedback: “Likely iron” is a guess, and the guess is wrong in the dangerous direction. Black, sticky stool on clopidogrel is a gate “yes”: hold the bolus and call.
choices.then: The nurse holds the syringe and asks you to check again. Standing, his pulse rises to 108; his hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL.

choices.text: Halve the bolus and stop his clopidogrel today.
choices.feedback: Neither is yours to change. The dose is the attending nephrologist’s decision, and stopping an antiplatelet drug eight months after a stent carries its own danger; never stop it yourself.
choices.then: The nurse holds the bolus and asks you to call. Standing, his pulse rises to 108; his hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL.

n2.prompt: What do you report to the attending nephrologist?

choices.text: Black stool for two days, clopidogrel and its last dose, the hemoglobin fall from 10.2 to 8.4, and his pulse rising on standing.
choices.feedback: The gate answer with details, the drug with its last dose, the trend against his own previous result, and what you saw. That lets the nephrologist decide on the heparin, the session and transfer in one call.
choices.then: The nephrologist orders a heparin-free session with saline flushes, a low fluid-removal goal, a laboratory hemoglobin, and transfer if he becomes unstable. Clopidogrel is left for the cardiologist and the gastroenterology team to decide.

choices.feedback: Too little to decide on. The nephrologist needs the drug and its last dose, the hemoglobin trend, and the vital signs.
choices.then: The nephrologist asks for the details, then orders a heparin-free session, a low fluid goal, a laboratory hemoglobin, and transfer if he becomes unstable.

choices.text: The black stool and today’s hemoglobin of 8.4, the two facts that most change whether heparin is safe, and ask what he wants done.
choices.feedback: The two key facts, but add clopidogrel with its last dose and his pulse on standing: both change how urgent this is.
choices.then: The nephrologist asks about blood thinners and vital signs, then orders a heparin-free session and transfer if he becomes unstable.

n3.scene: The nurse calls you. His pressure has fallen from 138/78 to 94/56 and his pulse is 116. Only 600 mL has been removed. He feels nauseated.
n3.prompt: What do you think, and what do you do?

choices.text: A fall bigger than 600 mL explains: likely ongoing bleeding. Stop fluid removal, lay him flat, call now, prepare transfer.
choices.feedback: When the pressure falls earlier and further than the fluid removed explains, think of a hidden bleed. Stop removal, support him by protocol, and call the nephrologist and the emergency team.

choices.text: Treat it as ordinary intradialytic hypotension: a saline bolus, then restart fluid removal at a lower rate.
choices.feedback: Six hundred milliliters does not explain this fall. Treating it as routine hypotension misses the likely cause: he is still bleeding.
choices.then: The pressure falls again to 90/54 within minutes. You stop removal, lay him flat and call.

choices.text: Stop fluid removal and recheck in 15 minutes.
choices.feedback: Stopping removal is right, but with a falling hemoglobin and a rising pulse, call now rather than after the recheck.
choices.then: At the recheck his pulse is still 114. You call the nephrologist.

n4.scene: The laboratory hemoglobin is 7.3 g/dL. He vomits a small amount of dark, coffee-ground material. The nephrologist asks you to end the session and transfer him. The circuit is intact; the last flush was clear.
n4.prompt: What about the blood in the circuit?

choices.feedback: Returning blood helps a bleeding patient. Do not return it only if the circuit has clotted, air or hemolysis is suspected, or the circuit has been opened. None applies here.

choices.text: Discard the circuit and disconnect quickly, so the transfer is not delayed.
choices.feedback: Returning blood takes minutes and gives back red cells he cannot spare. With an intact circuit, return it.

choices.text: Return it with a fast saline chase and an extra liter of saline afterward, to fill him up before the ambulance arrives.
choices.feedback: Return the blood by the usual method. Further fluid for a bleeding patient is a decision for the nephrologist and the receiving team, not a reflex.

n5.scene: Endoscopy found a bleeding ulcer, which was treated. The cardiologist restarted clopidogrel. Mr. Santos is back for his first session. The nurse asks which heparin order to use.

choices.text: Run the gate, and use the order the nephrologist writes for his return. Don’t default to the old one.
choices.feedback: Everything has changed since the old order: a treated ulcer, an antiplatelet drug restarted, a lower hemoglobin. The nephrologist decides the heparin order; you ask the gate questions every session.

choices.text: The usual bolus. The ulcer was treated.
choices.feedback: A treated ulcer does not reset the order. Ask the nephrologist, and run the gate.

choices.text: Heparin-free from now on, since he has bled once.
choices.feedback: Heparin-free dialysis is no guarantee of safety, and some of those sessions clot, which costs blood. It is the nephrologist’s decision.

end.title: The record
end.text: The chart shows the gate answer, the held bolus, the calls and who decided each step, the hemoglobin trend, the blood returned, and the transfer time. The unit adds “black stool?” to the spoken gate questions, with a note that iron does not rule out bleeding.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Ask the gate questions before every bolus. Any “yes” holds it until the nephrologist has heard.
  • Iron does not rule out blood. Black stool on a blood thinner is a “yes.”
  • A pressure fall bigger than the fluid removed may be a hidden bleed.
  • Return the blood to a bleeding patient when the circuit is intact.
  • Never stop a blood thinner yourself, and never change the heparin dose.

See The bleeding-risk check, Bleeding you cannot see and Blood thinners.
